title: Weekly, every two weeks or monthly: how often should your home be cleaned?
excerpt: It depends on pets, children and how much you cook. Here's how our customers decide.
content:
Most of our regular customers book every two weeks. But the right answer depends on how your home is lived in. Here's the rough guide we give people on the phone.

Weekly

For homes with dogs or cats that shed, small children, or someone with allergies. Dust and hair build up fast, and a weekly clean stops it settling into carpets and sofas. It's also 15% off every visit.

Every two weeks

The sweet spot for most couples and families. Kitchens and bathrooms never get past the point of a normal clean, and you can keep on top of the rest yourself in between.

Monthly

For tidy households, people who travel a lot, or anyone who just wants the deep work done: bathrooms descaled, floors done properly and the dust off the high shelves.

Not sure?

Start with a deep clean, then try every two weeks for a couple of months. You can change how often at any time with 48 hours' notice.

title: Moving out? Seven places landlords check that most people miss
excerpt: Inside the oven, the top of the fridge and the window tracks. The spots that cost people their deposit.
content:
We clean hundreds of homes a year for people moving out, and we've walked through plenty of inspections with property managers. These are the spots they always check.

1. Inside the oven

Baked-on grease is the most common deduction we see. It takes time: start the night before with a paste of baking soda and water.

2. Top of the fridge and behind it

Pull it out if you can. The dust and crumbs behind a fridge are a landlord favorite.

3. Window tracks and sills

Dead bugs and grit collect in the tracks. A vacuum crevice tool and an old toothbrush do the job.

4. Baseboards, doors and switches

Scuffs and fingerprints show up in an empty room. A damp microfiber cloth gets most of them off.

5. Bathroom grout and glass

Hard water leaves a white film on shower glass. Vinegar and patience, or a descaler, clears it.

6. Cabinets and drawers

Empty every one and wipe inside, including the shelves under the sink.

7. Photos

Take dated photos of every room when you're done. They're your proof if anything is disputed. We send them to you after every move-out clean.

title: Five habits for a bathroom that stays clean between visits
excerpt: A squeegee, an open window and two minutes a day. Small habits that keep mold and limescale away.
content:
Raleigh is humid, and bathrooms feel it first. These five habits keep yours fresh between cleans.

Squeegee the glass

Thirty seconds after each shower stops hard water spots before they start.

Run the fan or open a window

Leave the fan on for twenty minutes after a shower. Mold needs damp air, so take it away.

Wipe the sink at night

Toothpaste and soap scum are easy to wipe off fresh and hard to scrub off later.

Wash the bath mat weekly

It holds more moisture than anything else in the room.

Leave the deep work to us

Grout, descaling and the floor behind the toilet are what we're there for.

title: What we clean with, and why we stopped using bleach
excerpt: Plant-based cleaners, microfiber and hot water. What's in our caddy, and what isn't.
content:
Customers often ask what we use. Here's what's in every team's caddy, and why.

Microfiber, color-coded

Blue for glass and mirrors, green for kitchens, red for bathrooms. Never mixed, so bathroom germs never reach your kitchen counter.

Plant-based cleaners

They clean just as well for everyday dirt, they're safe around pets and children, and your home smells clean rather than of chemicals.

Why not bleach?

Bleach disinfects, but it doesn't clean dirt, it fades fabrics and it's harsh to breathe in a closed room. We use a hospital-grade disinfectant on toilets and handles instead.

A HEPA vacuum

It holds on to fine dust and pet dander instead of blowing it back into the room, which matters if anyone in the house has allergies.
